questions.question: How does Ishmael's attitude toward Queequeg change from his first night at the Spouter-Inn to the point where they become bosom friends?
questions.reference_answer: At first Ishmael is suspicious of Queequeg and resolves that the harpooneer must get into bed before he does. After the two share a pipe and a long conversation, Queequeg pledges friendship, and Ishmael admits that the savage has softened his bitterness toward the world.

evidence.quote: I could not help it, but I began to feel suspicious of this “dark complexioned” harpooneer. At any rate, I made up my mind that if it so turned out that we should sleep together, he must undress and get into bed before I did.
I felt a melting in me. No more my splintered heart and maddened hand were turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it.

and when our smoke was over, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me round the waist, and said that henceforth we were married; meaning, in his country’s phrase, that we were bosom friends; he would gladly die for me, if need should be.

questions.question: How do Starbuck and Stubb differ in their attitudes toward fear, courage and death in the whale fishery?
questions.reference_answer: Starbuck is a cautious, superstitious Quaker who values courage only as a useful tool and refuses to let anyone in his boat who is not afraid of a whale. Stubb, by contrast, handles deadly chases with an easy, indifferent humor and is never clearly shown to think about death at all.

evidence.quote: “I will have no man in my boat,” said Starbuck, “who is not afraid of a whale.”
Starbuck was no crusader after perils; in him courage was not a sentiment; but a thing simply useful to him, and always at hand upon all mortally practical occasions.

A happy-go-lucky; neither craven nor valiant; taking perils as they came with an indifferent air; and while engaged in the most imminent crisis of the chase, toiling away, calm and collected as a journeyman joiner engaged for the year.
What he thought of death itself, there is no telling.

questions.question: Why does Ahab become so moody and grim by the time the Pequod is at sea, and what is the cause that the text connects to his condition?
questions.reference_answer: Peleg attributes Ahab's moodiness to the loss of his leg to a whale, along with the sharp shooting pains of his bleeding stump. When the Pequod sails, Ahab appears on deck with a face of 'crucifixion' and a 'mighty woe', showing that the old injury has left a lasting, brooding grief.

evidence.quote: I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg last voyage by that accursed whale, he’s been a kind of moody—desperate moody, and savage sometimes; but that will all pass off.
it was the sharp shooting pains in his bleeding stump that brought that about, as any one might see.
And not only that, but moody stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face; in all the nameless regal overbearing dignity of some mighty woe.

questions.question: How does Ishmael's view of Yojo's plan for choosing the ship change from the moment Queequeg proposes it to the moment the Pequod is signed?
questions.reference_answer: Ishmael initially rejects Queequeg's plan to let Yojo choose the vessel, having wanted Queequeg's judgment instead. Yet he sets out to find a ship, inspects the Pequod, and decides it is the right one, and in the end he is content that the Pequod is the very ship Yojo had provided.

evidence.quote: Now, this plan of Queequeg’s, or rather Yojo’s, touching the selection of our craft; I did not like that plan at all.
and finally, going on board the Pequod, looked around her for a moment, and then decided that this was the very ship for us.

And, after signing the papers, off I went; nothing doubting but that I had done a good morning’s work, and that the Pequod was the identical ship that Yojo had provided to carry Queequeg and me round the Cape.

questions.question: How does the relationship between the two owners, Peleg and Bildad, move from open hostility at the start of the voyage's preparations to an affectionate parting at Nantucket?
questions.reference_answer: During the ship's outfitting, Peleg and Bildad quarrel furiously, with Peleg threatening Bildad and Bildad warning him of the fiery pit. At departure, however, Bildad clings to Peleg's hand and gazes at him, and Peleg is near to tears, so their bitter rivalry gives way to genuine old-shipmate fondness.

evidence.quote: “Thou Bildad!” roared Peleg, starting up and clattering about the cabin. “Blast ye, Captain Bildad, if I had followed thy advice in these matters, I would afore now had a conscience to lug about that would be heavy enough to founder the largest ship that ever sailed round Cape Horn.”
convulsively grasped stout Peleg by the hand, and holding up a lantern, for a moment stood gazing heroically in his face
As for Peleg himself, he took it more like a philosopher; but for all his philosophy, there was a tear twinkling in his eye, when the lantern came too near.

questions.question: How does Ishmael's judgment of the ragged prophet Elijah shift from the wharf conversation to the moment Elijah questions them about the men on the ship?
questions.reference_answer: Ishmael first dismisses Elijah as a humbug and a bugbear after their wharf encounter, and tries to forget him. But when Elijah reappears at dawn and asks whether they saw men heading toward the ship, Ishmael grows unsettled and is no longer able to dismiss him so easily.

evidence.quote: Elijah! thought I, and we walked away, both commenting, after each other’s fashion, upon this ragged old sailor; and agreed that he was nothing but a humbug, trying to be a bugbear.
“Did ye see anything looking like men going towards that ship a while ago?”
Struck by this plain matter-of-fact question, I answered, saying, “Yes, I thought I did see four or five men; but it was too dim to be sure.”

questions.question: How does Ahab's relationship to the white whale change from the quarter-deck speech, where the crew learns of Moby Dick's role in his injury, to the later account of his monomania?
questions.reference_answer: At the quarter-deck Ahab openly admits that Moby Dick took his leg and vows to chase the whale around the world, which is still framed as a personal grievance. Later the narrator explains that Ahab came to identify the whale with all his bodily woes and with the malice of the world, piling the hate of his whole race onto it. The grievance thus grows from a specific injury into a totalizing obsession.

evidence.quote: “Aye, aye! it was that accursed white whale that razeed me; made a poor pegging lubber of me for ever and a day!” Then tossing both arms, with measureless imprecations he shouted out: “Aye, aye! and I’ll chase him round Good Hope, and round the Horn

He piled upon the whale’s white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down; and then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart’s shell upon it.

questions.question: Ahab tells the crew that his vengeance is worth a premium, but later the narrator shows him privately worrying about the crew's money. How do these two positions differ?
questions.reference_answer: In the quarter-deck scene Ahab presents his vengeance as a higher currency that outvalues Nantucket profit, dismissing Starbuck's concern about barrels. In the chapter on surmises, however, Ahab reasons that the crew must have cash as well, since a purely romantic quest would drive men away. The public rhetoric of pure vengeance is thus contradicted by his private calculation of wages and profit.

evidence.quote: How many barrels will thy vengeance yield thee even if thou gettest it, Captain Ahab? it will not fetch thee much in our Nantucket market.”

Nantucket market! Hoot! But come closer, Starbuck; thou requirest a little lower layer. If money’s to be the measurer, man, and the accountants have computed their great counting-house the globe, by girdling it with guineas, one to every three parts of an inch; then, let me tell thee, that my vengeance will fetch a great premium

I will not strip these men, thought Ahab, of all hopes of cash—aye, cash. They may scorn cash now; but let some months go by, and no perspective promise of it to them, and then this same quiescent cash all at once mutinying in them, this same cash would soon cashier Ahab.

questions.question: Why does Ahab keep the Pequod performing ordinary whaling duties and maintaining mast-head watches, even though his real purpose is the white whale?
questions.reference_answer: Ahab openly announced his private purpose at the quarter-deck, which exposed him to the charge that he had usurped command, and the crew could in principle refuse him. To protect his authority he must keep the ship's nominal, customary business going. That is why he keeps hailing the mast-heads to report even a porpoise.

evidence.quote: Having impulsively, it is probable, and perhaps somewhat prematurely revealed the prime but private purpose of the Pequod’s voyage, Ahab was now entirely conscious that, in so doing, he had indirectly laid himself open to the unanswerable charge of usurpation
And this is what ye have shipped for, men! to chase that white whale on both sides of land, and over all sides of earth, till he spouts black blood and rolls fin out.
Ahab plainly saw that he must still in a good degree continue true to the natural, nominal purpose of the Pequod’s voyage

questions.question: How does the crew's commitment to the hunt change from Ahab's first offer of the gold ounce to the moment the harpooneers swear the oath over the harpoon-sockets?
questions.reference_answer: The hunt begins as a bounty: Ahab holds up a gold ounce and promises it to whoever first sights the white whale, and the crew cheers as the coin is nailed to the mast. The bounty then becomes a ritual pact, as the mates and harpooneers drink from the harpoon-sockets and swear an oath of 'Death to Moby Dick'. The commitment moves from a reward for sighting to a sworn, blood-bound vow.

evidence.quote: Look ye! d’ye see this Spanish ounce of gold?”—holding up a broad bright coin to the sun—“it is a sixteen dollar piece, men.
Drink, ye harpooneers! drink and swear, ye men that man the deathful whaleboat’s bow—Death to Moby Dick!

questions.question: According to the text, which vessel was sunk by a whale in 1820, what was her captain's name, and what sea was she cruising in?
questions.reference_answer: The ship Essex, commanded by Captain Pollard of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean in 1820. A whale rammed her and she sank.

evidence.quote: In the year 1820 the ship Essex, Captain Pollard, of Nantucket, was cruising in the Pacific Ocean.

questions.question: How does Starbuck's stance toward Ahab change from the Captain's dinner, where he is deferential, to the chapter called Dusk, where he admits he is trapped by Ahab?
questions.reference_answer: At dinner Starbuck takes his meat from Ahab 'as though receiving alms', showing servile deference to the captain. By the Dusk chapter, after the oath and the crew's frenzy, he is bound to Ahab against his conscience, describing his duty as 'to obey, rebelling'. His deference has become a reluctant, resentful submission.

evidence.quote: the mate received his meat as though receiving alms; and cut it tenderly; and a little started if, perchance, the knife grazed against the plate
My soul is more than matched; she’s overmanned; and by a madman! Insufferable sting, that sanity should ground arms on such a field!
Oh! I plainly see my miserable office,—to obey, rebelling; and worse yet, to hate with touch of pity!

questions.question: How does the image of the sperm whale's head as a riddle or Sphinx develop from Ahab's first address to it to the later chapters on its brow and brain?
questions.reference_answer: Ahab first sees the hanging head as the Sphynx in the desert and demands that it speak its secret. Later the narrator says the whale's brow is a riddle that cannot be read, and in the phrenology chapter calls the whale a Sphinx, whose brain is hidden behind its outworks. The enigma is thus carried from Ahab's apostrophe into the narrator's own attempts at reading the whale.

evidence.quote: It was a black and hooded head; and hanging there in the midst of so intense a calm, it seemed the Sphynx’s in the desert.
I but put that brow before you. Read it if you can.
If the Sperm Whale be physiognomically a Sphinx, to the phrenologist his brain seems that geometrical circle which it is impossible to square.

questions.question: How does the image of the whale-line and bondage change from the warning that all men are born with halters round their necks, to the Siamese tie between Ishmael and Queequeg, to the closing claim that every reader is a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish?
questions.reference_answer: The line first stands for the mortal dangers all men live with, given as halters around the neck. In the monkey-rope chapter it becomes a bond that ties Ishmael to Queequeg, so that one man's fate depends on the other. The final chapter on Fast-Fish and Loose-Fish applies the same idea of possession and dependence to the reader.

evidence.quote: But why say more? All men live enveloped in whale-lines. All are born with halters round their necks; but it is only when caught in the swift, sudden turn of death, that mortals realize the silent, subtle, ever-present perils of life.
So, then, an elongated Siamese ligature united us.
What is the great globe itself but a Loose-Fish? And what are you, reader, but a Loose-Fish and a Fast-Fish, too?

questions.question: How does the scene of the sharks and birds feeding on the dead whale move from the night of the Sabbath feast into the mournful image of a funeral?
questions.reference_answer: On the night the whale is moored, thousands of sharks feast on it like diners at a banquet. In the funeral chapter the narrator recasts the same feeding as a mock funeral, with sea-vultures in mourning and air-sharks in black, and he turns it into a reflection on the vultureism of the world. The feast becomes a funeral procession.

evidence.quote: Mingling their mumblings with his own mastications, thousands on thousands of sharks, swarming round the dead leviathan, smackingly feasted on its fatness.
There’s a most doleful and most mocking funeral! The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all punctiliously in black or speckled.

questions.question: How does the narrator's judgment of the dignity of the sperm whale's head differ from his judgment of the right whale's head?
questions.reference_answer: The narrator first ranks the sperm whale's head above the right whale's for pervading dignity and character. Later he jokingly calls the right whale a sulky king who is ill-suited to a diadem. The right whale is thus treated as the less noble of the two.

evidence.quote: As you behold it, you involuntarily yield the immense superiority to him, in point of pervading dignity.
But if this whale be a king, he is a very sulky looking fellow to grace a diadem.

questions.question: Why does the Pequod come close to capsizing when the sinking whale is still tied to her, and what role does Starbuck play in it?
questions.reference_answer: The ship is already strained, with the heavy sperm whale head on one side. The Right whale carcass then sinks and drags the ship over sideways. Starbuck holds on to the carcass so stubbornly that the ship nearly turns over before the fasteners break.

evidence.quote: In good time, Flask’s saying proved true. As before, the Pequod steeply leaned over towards the sperm whale’s head, now, by the counterpoise of both heads, she regained her even keel; though sorely strained, you may well believe.

However, Starbuck, who had the ordering of affairs, hung on to it to the last; hung on to it so resolutely, indeed, that when at length the ship would have been capsized, if still persisting in locking arms with the body
But a sudden stop was put to further discoveries, by the ship’s being unprecedentedly dragged over sideways to the sea, owing to the body’s immensely increasing tendency to sink.

questions.question: How does Stubb's idea about the ambergris change from a passing remark to a scheme and then to the actual salvage?
questions.reference_answer: Stubb first wonders aloud whether the captain has thought of the ambergris, and decides it is worth trying. He then forms a plan with the Guernsey-man to deceive the French captain, with the mate speaking for him as an interpreter. The scheme succeeds when Stubb cuts into the whale and finds the ambergris, and the captain's order to desist comes only after the haul.

evidence.quote: I wonder now if our old man has thought of that. It’s worth trying.

According to this little plan of theirs, the Guernsey-man, under cover of an interpreter’s office, was to tell the Captain what he pleased, but as coming from Stubb; and as for Stubb, he was to utter any nonsense that should come uppermost in him during the interview.
Presently a breeze sprang up; Stubb feigned to cast off from the whale; hoisting his boats, the Frenchman soon increased his distance, while the Pequod slid in between him and Stubb’s whale.

questions.question: How does Pip's fate develop from the moment Stubb abandons him at sea to his later bond with Ahab?
questions.reference_answer: Stubb's ruthless order to stay in the boat leaves Pip adrift, and the ship's rescue leaves him permanently changed, so that the crew think him an idiot. Much later, Ahab takes the mad boy into his own cabin, making the same castaway who was abandoned the one person Ahab feels bound to.

evidence.quote: “Stick to the boat, Pip, or by the Lord, I won’t pick you up if you jump; mind that.
By the merest chance the ship itself at last rescued him; but from that hour the little negro went about the deck an idiot; such, at least, they said he was.

unlocated_quotes: “Here, boy; Ahab’s cabin shall be Pip’s home henceforth, while Ahab lives.

questions.question: How does Queequeg's coffin change from a sea-chest and an offering for his death into a life-buoy?
questions.reference_answer: Queequeg, believing he is dying, has the carpenter build him a coffin, which he then uses as a sea-chest and carves. Later, with no cask light enough for a life-buoy, the crew turn the same coffin into the ship's buoy, which Starbuck reacts to with shock.

evidence.quote: Now, when this strange circumstance was made known aft, the carpenter was at once commanded to do Queequeg’s bidding, whatever it might include.
by certain strange signs and inuendoes Queequeg hinted a hint concerning his coffin.
“A life-buoy of a coffin!” cried Starbuck, starting.

questions.question: Why does Starbuck take up the loaded musket in the cabin during the typhoon, and why does he finally put it back?
questions.reference_answer: Starbuck's impulse to shoot Ahab grows from Ahab's earlier act of aiming a loaded musket at him, and from the fear that Ahab will drag the crew to doom in the storm. Starbuck finds no lawful way to stop him and ultimately cannot bring himself to fire, so he returns the musket to its rack.

evidence.quote: Ahab seized a loaded musket from the rack (forming part of most South-Sea-men’s cabin furniture), and pointing it towards Starbuck, exclaimed:
“He would have shot me once,” he murmured, “yes, there’s the very musket that he pointed at me;
Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; but turning from the door, he placed the death-tube in its rack, and left the place.

questions.question: Contrast Ahab's cold rejection of the Rachel's captain with his later tearful, tender moment on the calm sea.
questions.reference_answer: When the Rachel's captain begs for help searching for his lost son, Ahab coldly refuses and retreats below. Later, in the calm, Ahab weeps and speaks tenderly of his own wife and child, showing a humanity he denied the grieving father.

evidence.quote: Hurriedly turning, with averted face, he descended into his cabin, leaving the strange captain transfixed at this unconditional and utter rejection of his so earnest suit.
From beneath his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop.

questions.question: How does the harpoon Ahab orders from Perth change from a request for an unbreakable weapon into an instrument he believes holds the whale's death?
questions.reference_answer: Ahab first orders Perth to forge a harpoon that a thousand fiends could not part, using horseshoe nail-stubs, and Ahab insists on welding it himself. Its barbs are tempered in the blood of the crew, and when the Pequod meets the Delight, Ahab brandishes it as the weapon that will kill the White Whale, claiming its death is in his hand.

evidence.quote: “I, too, want a harpoon made; one that a thousand yoke of fiends could not part, Perth;
“Ego non baptizo te in nomine patris, sed in nomine diaboli!”
“Look ye, Nantucketer; here in this hand I hold his death! Tempered in blood, and tempered by lightning are these barbs;

questions.question: How does the doubloon change from a talisman the crew revere to a prize Ahab claims as his own?
questions.reference_answer: At first the doubloon is a sanctified talisman, revered by the crew as the white whale's emblem and guarded from theft. Later, Ahab claims it as his own, reserving it for himself as the prize of his pursuit and offering it only to whoever kills the whale.

evidence.quote: however wanton in their sailor ways, one and all, the mariners revered it as the white whale’s talisman.
“Not the same instant; not the same—no, the doubloon is mine, Fate reserved the doubloon for me.

questions.question: How does Ahab's response to the Parsee's prophecy change from the moment the Parsee vanishes to the moment his body is seen tied to the whale?
questions.reference_answer: When the Parsee disappears, Ahab treats the prophecy that the Parsee would go before him, yet be seen again, as a riddle that 'pecks my brain' and vows to solve it. When the Parsee's torn body appears lashed to the whale, Ahab accepts that the prophecy has come true, calls it the 'hearse' the Parsee promised, and treats it as a fulfilment he must still follow to the end.

evidence.quote: “Befooled, befooled!”—drawing in a long lean breath—“Aye, Parsee! I see thee again.—Aye, and thou goest before; and this, _this_ then is the hearse that thou didst promise.

unlocated_quotes: “The Parsee—the Parsee!—gone, gone? and he was to go before:—but still was to be seen again ere I could perish—How’s that?—There’s a riddle now might baffle all the lawyers backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges:—like a hawk’s beak it pecks my brain.

questions.question: How do Ahab and Starbuck each justify their obedience, and how do their accounts of who they are obeying differ?
questions.reference_answer: Ahab presents himself as the Fates' lieutenant who acts under orders and expects his crew to obey him. Starbuck, by contrast, frames the same obedience as a possible betrayal of God, saying he fears he disobeys God by obeying Ahab. The two men thus locate final authority in different places: Ahab in fate, Starbuck in God.

evidence.quote: Fool! I am the Fates’ lieutenant; I act under orders. Look thou, underling! that thou obeyest mine.
“God keep us, but already my bones feel damp within me, and from the inside wet my flesh. I misdoubt me that I disobey my God in obeying him!”

questions.question: Why does the Pequod ultimately go down, given the warnings that Starbuck gives during the chase?
questions.reference_answer: Starbuck repeatedly urges Ahab to stop the chase on the third day, arguing that Ahab, not the whale, is the one who is seeking destruction. Ahab refuses and keeps steering the ship after the whale, which brings the whale into a collision with the ship's bow. The ram stove in the hull, and the Pequod sinks as a result of Ahab's refusal to desist.

evidence.quote: “Oh! Ahab,” cried Starbuck, “not too late is it, even now, the third day, to desist. See! Moby Dick seeks thee not. It is thou, thou, that madly seekest him!”
Oh, Ahab, Ahab, lo, thy work. Steady! helmsman, steady.

questions.question: How does Ahab's plan for his boats change from the morning after the first broken boat to the moment he sends the others back to the ship on the third day?
questions.reference_answer: After the first wreck, Ahab orders the spare boats rigged and the crews mustered to continue the pursuit with a full complement. On the third day, after the Parsee's body is found and the boats are destroyed, he tells the crew to return to the ship and repair the boats if they can, leaving only himself and the chase. His plan shifts from a whole fleet of boats to Ahab alone, with the others sent back.

evidence.quote: Up helm, then; pile on the sail again, ship keepers! down the rest of the spare boats and rig them—Mr. Starbuck away, and muster the boat’s crews.
Away, mates, to the ship! those boats are useless now; repair them if ye can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die—Down, men!

questions.question: How does Starbuck's appeal to Ahab change from the moment he first begs him to stop hunting the whale to his final plea as Ahab's boat leaves the ship?
questions.reference_answer: Early on, Starbuck argues against further pursuit, calling it devil's madness and warning that the whale will swamp the crew. As Ahab departs on the third day, his appeal becomes personal and emotional: he cries 'Oh, my captain, my captain!' and begs him not to go, saying that a brave man's weeping shows how great the agony of the persuasion is. He moves from reasoned argument to pleading with tears, and Ahab refuses both times.

evidence.quote: “Great God! but for one single instant show thyself,” cried Starbuck; “never, never wilt thou capture him, old man—In Jesus’ name no more of this, that’s worse than devil’s madness.
“Oh, my captain, my captain!—noble heart—go not—go not!—see, it’s a brave man that weeps; how great the agony of the persuasion then!”

questions.question: How does the coffin, which Ahab rejects as his own fate, reappear in the epilogue, and what does that reversal reveal?
questions.reference_answer: Ahab, before the final chase, declares that no coffin or hearse can be his and that only hemp can kill him, and the line then catches him round the neck and pulls him from the boat. In the epilogue, the coffin life-buoy is what keeps Ishmael afloat for a day and a night, so the coffin Ahab refused becomes the means of survival for the one man who escapes. The reversal shows the fate Ahab tried to avoid falling on him and sparing another.

evidence.quote: “Drive, drive in your nails, oh ye waves! to their uttermost heads drive them in! ye but strike a thing without a lid; and no coffin and no hearse can be mine:—and hemp only can kill me! Ha! ha!”
but the flying turn caught him round the neck,
Buoyed up by that coffin, for almost one whole day and night, I floated on a soft and dirgelike main.
